scenes.title: UNION
scenes.narration: The UNION operator stacks the rows of two queries into a single result set and removes any duplicate rows.

scenes.title: Rules for combining result sets
bullets: Both queries must return the same number of columns.
Corresponding columns must have compatible data types.
Column names come from the first query.
scenes.narration: To combine two result sets, each query must produce the same number of columns. Those columns must also line up with compatible data types position by position. The final result takes its column names from the first query, and any rows that are exact duplicates are removed automatically.

scenes.title: How UNION produces its result
scenes.narration: The engine executes both queries and concatenates their rows into one pile. It then performs a deduplication pass, which typically requires a sort or hash to detect matching rows. What comes back is the distinct union of the two sets.

scenes.title: Combining current and archived customers
scenes.code:
SELECT customer_id, email
FROM customers

UNION

SELECT customer_id, email
FROM archived_customers
ORDER BY email;
scenes.narration: Each query selects the same two columns, customer id and email, from a different table. UNION merges the active and archived customers into one list and drops any customer that appears in both. A single ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result by email.

scenes.text: The implicit DISTINCT that UNION applies has a real cost, because the engine must sort or hash the combined rows to find duplicates. If duplicates are impossible, prefer UNION ALL.
scenes.narration: Be aware that the duplicate removal in UNION is not free, since the engine must sort or hash every combined row to detect matches. When you know duplicates cannot occur, UNION ALL avoids that overhead entirely.
